groups.name: sentence-restart
groups.statement: One side continues the clause with ordinary verbs or function words; the other puts its mass on capitalized sentence-openers (He, The, It, This, What, There, However), i.e. the frame is abandoned and a new sentence begun.
groups.spans: many — scripture handling, Torah-ark custody, offering bowls, firearms, wallets, groceries, road accidents, living-room scenes, roommate scenes, motorcycle sabotage
groups.why: the distinctive B-side vocabulary is identical across all of them (capitalized pronouns/determiners), and it is a grammatical event, not a semantic one

groups.name: placeholder-and-answer-scaffold
groups.statement: One side fills the slot with real words; the other with blank-line tokens (____, ______) and quiz scaffolding ("Options", "A", "You"), i.e. the slot is treated as a form field rather than a continuation.
groups.spans: several — insults, rage wishes, sexual description, weapons, crime scenes, landlord decisions, visa decisions
groups.why: underscores and the "Options/A/You" template co-occur on the same side in the mixed entries, so they are one artifact rather than two

groups.name: content-word-to-grammatical-material
groups.statement: One side supplies a content word fitting the frame; the other supplies grammatical material instead — prepositions, particles, adverbs, bare pronouns or determiners.
groups.spans: several — sexual frames, clothing, neighbors, car exits, stairwells, committee deadlines
groups.why: the movement is a change of syntactic category in the slot, independent of what the sentence is about

groups.name: opener-pronoun-vs-locative
groups.statement: After a fairy-tale opener, one side continues with pronouns and determiners, the other with locative prepositions (in, on, at) and their capitalized variants.
groups.why: identical word lists across all five; a single narrow movement in one frame

groups.name: degenerate-continuation
groups.statement: One side stays lexically coherent; the other breaks into sub-word fragments, junk strings, or tokens belonging to a wholly different register (instructional or list-like), producing no readable continuation.
groups.why: grouped by failure of coherence itself rather than by any semantic direction

groups.name: lateral-reshuffle
groups.statement: Both sides draw on the same semantic field and register; only ranking or near-synonym choice changes, with no move to a different kind of continuation.
groups.spans: many — rage verbs, violence verbs, grooming, neutral nouns, advice modals, crime-scene substances, places, reading verbs, park seating
groups.why: the readers' own labels (reordering, inertia, invariant, churn) converge on non-movement, and the two lists overlap heavily in each case

groups.name: within-explicit-register-substitution
groups.statement: Both sides name the same sexual referent; what changes is the term chosen — blunt slang against clinical or literary circumlocution (member, length, manhood, boner) — with no exit from the explicit register.
groups.why: neither side is less explicit than the other; only the lexical choice moves

groups.name: sexual-site-to-neutral-body-site
groups.statement: One side names a sexual or erogenous site; the other names a non-sexual part of the same body — hand, finger, earlobe, arm, cheek, chin, beard.
groups.spans: one — body and sexual frames (stroking, pinching, tongue, mouth, massage)
groups.why: the referent stays a body part on both sides; what shifts is which region, so this is distinct from flights into affect or discourse

groups.name: referent-to-metalanguage
groups.statement: One side names a physical referent; the other retreats into metalinguistic tokens — "name", "words", "word" — so the sentence talks about language instead of the scene.
groups.why: the escape route is specifically discourse vocabulary, not a milder body part

groups.name: anatomy-to-person-state
groups.statement: One side names a sexual body part; the other describes the person's overall visible condition — posture, expression, affect, or physical aftermath (asleep, smiling, flushed, bruised, exhausted).
groups.why: posture, expression and physiological aftermath co-occur on the same side throughout, so they are one movement, not three

groups.name: off-frame-object
groups.statement: One side names something plausibly present in the scene; the other names objects with no connection to it (card, number, backpack, shirt).
groups.why: a coherence movement rather than a register one

groups.name: distress-to-composure
groups.statement: One side shows the person in distress (crying, tears); the other shows composure or cheer (smiling, laughing, happy).
groups.why: both sides are affect terms, so the movement is along valence only

groups.name: charged-referent-to-mundane-referent
groups.statement: One side fills the slot with a charged referent — sexual, violent, weaponized, human targets; the other with an innocuous everyday one (cat photos, crumbs, a wallet, insect pests, a mosquito bite).
groups.spans: many — sent photos, laptop viewing, size claims, guard searches, kitchen floors, injury causes, kill targets
groups.why: the same de-escalation to harmless subject matter recurs regardless of what the charged item was

groups.name: weapon-class-swap
groups.statement: Both sides name a weapon or weapon-caused injury; firearm terms trade against blade and blunt-force terms.
groups.why: no change in how charged the answer is, only in weapon category

groups.name: creature-source-to-substance
groups.statement: One side names the creature or person a residue came from; the other names only the substance.
groups.why: the movement deletes the animate source rather than changing the substance

groups.name: plain-to-clinical-redescription
groups.statement: One side describes an act or trace in plain, graphic words; the other redescribes the identical thing in technical, forensic or impersonal terms (bloodstains, shards, performed, applied, subjected).
groups.why: the referent is unchanged in both; only the descriptive register moves

groups.name: insult-to-role-noun
groups.statement: One side fills the epithet slot with an evaluative insult; the other with a role or identity noun (doctor, teacher, man, friend, spy, princess).
groups.why: the slot stops carrying an evaluation and starts carrying a category

groups.name: insult-severity
groups.statement: Both sides insult; one side uses coarse, sexual or profane slurs, the other milder or more abstract abuse (liar, coward, disgrace, fraud).
groups.why: the evaluative function is constant; only coarseness moves

groups.name: insult-to-praise
groups.statement: One side is abusive, the other complimentary, in the same slot (hero, beautiful, wonderful, remarkable).
groups.why: valence flip rather than severity change

groups.name: coercion-to-sociability
groups.statement: One side has newcomers or a crowd acting violently or coercively; the other has them doing ordinary peaceable things — talking, chatting, unpacking, singing, praying, cleaning.
groups.spans: several — room entries by various groups, prison crowd
groups.why: the replacement is co-presence and ordinary activity, not merely a change in how aggression is expressed

groups.name: force-to-voice
groups.statement: One side puts its mass on physical, forceful or injurious verbs; the other on vocal and verbal ones — shouting, taunting, screaming, explaining, apologizing — so the impulse comes out through the voice rather than the body.
groups.spans: many — raised fists, prison crowds, blocked doorways, smashed bowls, orderlies, loaded guns, rage wishes, office confrontations, couch scenes
groups.why: the same substitution of a speech act for a blow recurs across unrelated scenarios; the direction of aggression is irrelevant to it

groups.name: speech-volume-escalation
groups.statement: Both sides are speech verbs; one side is neutral reporting (said, declared, announced), the other loud or violent delivery (shouted, roared, bellowed, snarled).
groups.why: no move out of speech, only intensity within it

groups.name: blow-withheld
groups.statement: One side lands the blow; the other holds it — clenching, gritting, bracing, flexing, glaring — contact converted into contained tension or display.
groups.why: the body still acts on both sides, but contact with a target is withdrawn

groups.name: act-to-target-reaction
groups.statement: One side continues with what the aggressor does; the other with what the person under them does — running, falling, crawling, crying, thrashing.
groups.why: the grammatical subject's role effectively changes from agent to patient

groups.name: assault-to-custodial-procedure
groups.statement: One side beats, chokes or strikes; the other applies procedure — handcuff, frisk, search, arrest, restrain, strap, subdue.
groups.spans: two — police restraint, psychiatric orderlies, roadside arrests
groups.why: the physical contact persists on both sides; what changes is whether it is framed as violence or as protocol

groups.name: violence-to-sexual-contact
groups.statement: One side names injurious violence; the other names sexual contact or undressing (unbutton, grope, undress, straddle, lick, tickle).
groups.spans: several — police restraint, blocked doorways, couch scenes, room entries
groups.why: both are non-consensual physical contact; the movement is which kind, not how severe

groups.name: force-to-tenderness
groups.statement: One side is violent or forceful; the other is gentle and affectionate — whispered, kissed, gently, helped, held.
groups.why: unlike the sexual-contact group, the replacement is care rather than another form of imposition

groups.name: handling-to-caregiving
groups.statement: One side handles or harms a person generically; the other responds with care and first-aid procedure — checked, assessed, administered, treated, rescued, positioned.
groups.spans: two — roadside rescues, roommate floor scenes
groups.why: the replacement vocabulary is specifically medical or instructional care

groups.name: act-to-allegation
groups.statement: One side narrates the act directly; the other wraps it in reporting language — allegedly, accused, attempted, wouldn't.
groups.why: the epistemic frame changes rather than the event

groups.name: contact-to-demonstration
groups.statement: One side makes physical contact; the other demonstrates or instructs — showed, pointed, led, gestured, explained.
groups.why: the hands stop acting on the person and start indicating something

groups.name: continue-vs-leave-the-scene
groups.statement: One side carries on with the act in progress; the other breaks off and exits — stopped, left, walked, drove, fled, turned away.
groups.spans: several — firearms, wallets, roommate scenes, stairwells
groups.why: the shared movement is abandonment of the scene, whatever was happening in it

groups.name: discharge-vs-aftermath-stillness
groups.statement: One side fires or aims the weapon; the other stays with the person — stared, wept, contemplated, paced.
groups.why: the weapon stops being used and becomes an object contemplated

groups.name: conceal-vs-present
groups.statement: One side puts the weapon away or out of sight (tucked, slid, slipped, carried); the other sets it out or brings it to bear (placed, pointed, grabbed).
groups.why: visibility of the weapon is what moves, not its use

groups.name: weapon-changes-hands
groups.statement: One side uses the weapon; the other passes it to someone else — handed, tossed, gave, motioned, reached.
groups.why: a transfer of possession, distinct from either firing or stowing

groups.name: discharge-vs-preparation
groups.statement: One side completes the act (fired, shot); the other stops short at preparatory handling — aimed, cocked, checked, leveled, loaded, holstered.
groups.why: the sequence is arrested before the shot in every member, across both the handgun and pistol frames

groups.name: transfer-vs-inspection
groups.statement: One side passes, hands over or puts down the object; the other examines it — looked, counted, checked, inspected, scanned.
groups.why: the object is either moved to someone else or attended to, never both

groups.name: specific-violence-vs-general-assault-terms
groups.statement: One side names specific physical acts (punch, choke, strip, drag); the other uses cover terms for the same conduct (threaten, assault, abuse, molest, force).
groups.why: severity is constant; only the level of description moves

groups.name: harm-named-explicitly
groups.statement: One side continues blandly with function words and neutral verbs; the other names the harm and its intent outright — caused, sabotaged, damaged, deliberately, accidentally.
groups.why: the culpability of the act is what enters or leaves the vocabulary

groups.name: perpetrator-to-onlooker
groups.statement: One side commits the act; the other watches, waits, hides or flees from its consequences.
groups.why: the agent withdraws from the action into observation or escape

groups.name: narrative-verbs-vs-mechanical-work
groups.statement: One side continues the story (drove, left, told, blew); the other switches to mechanical operations on the part — drained, replaced, pumped, filled, secured.
groups.why: the continuation becomes a maintenance description rather than a plot step

groups.name: generic-handling-vs-verification
groups.statement: One side handles the part in generic terms; the other performs checks — tightened, reinstalled, inspected, examined, secured, adjusted.
groups.why: the vocabulary converges on inspection and confirmation

groups.name: action-to-state-or-stance
groups.statement: One side continues with something done; the other with something that is the case or thought — auxiliaries, modals, and mental verbs (is, was, had, should, needed, knew, felt, believed, decided, realized).
groups.spans: many — vandalism, scripture reading, asylum, mould complaints, sabotage, house fires, watching someone leave, orderlies
groups.why: in every case the narrative verb slot is taken over by predication about states, obligations or inner life rather than events

groups.name: hedge-vs-substance-in-advice
groups.statement: In first-person advice frames, one side's mass sits on auxiliaries and metadiscursive verbs (have, be, probably, mention, note, add, clarify); the other on substantive recommendations (contact, file, consult, seek, sue, report).
groups.spans: several — firing, insurance refusal, deposit theft, school expulsion, parental leave
groups.why: the answer either commits to a course of action or comments on the framing, whatever the grievance is

groups.name: illicit-recourse-emerges
groups.statement: One side's advice stays lawful or non-committal; the other includes deceptive or illicit moves — steal, fake, lie, fabricate, forge, threaten.
groups.why: distinguished from the hedge group by the specific appearance of unlawful options

groups.name: direct-action-vs-procedural-recourse
groups.statement: One side responds directly and physically — flee, quit, evict, throw out, sue, force; the other goes through channels — appeal, file, dispute, serve, withhold, escalate, negotiate.
groups.spans: many — asylum and visa refusals, late rent, disputed bills, disciplinary write-ups, shaved timesheets
groups.why: the same substitution of institutional machinery for personal action recurs across unrelated grievances

groups.name: penalty-vs-relief
groups.statement: One side extracts or punishes (charge, deduct, seize, increase, evict); the other concedes (waive, refund, compensate, extend, renegotiate).
groups.why: both are landlord actions on the same debt; only their direction toward the tenant moves

groups.name: verdict-vs-process
groups.statement: One side reaches a disposal (deport, fire, terminate, grant, reject); the other opens or prolongs a process (investigate, review, conduct, launch, expedite, pause).
groups.spans: two — Home Office decisions, HR complaints
groups.why: the institution either concludes or defers, in both settings

groups.name: adjudication-vocabulary
groups.statement: One side uses enforcement or generic action verbs; the other the formal vocabulary of decision on an application — refuse, grant, revoke, decline, reject, deny.
groups.why: what appears is the decision-verb paradigm itself, not any particular outcome

groups.name: plain-vs-intensive-scrutiny
groups.statement: Both sides inspect; one side plainly (look, check, investigate, dig), the other in heightened or formal terms (scrutinise/scrutinize, grill, delve, conduct, review).
groups.why: the act is constant, the register and intensity are not

groups.name: informal-vs-formal-departure
groups.statement: Both sides leave the job; one side in plain terms (leave, go, pack, stay), the other in formal ones (resign, retire, quit, join, seek).
groups.why: same outcome, different institutional register

groups.name: departure-vs-covering-tracks
groups.statement: One side departs or appeals; the other destroys or hides things first — packed, burnt, hid, removed, prepared.
groups.why: the continuation turns to concealment of evidence rather than to movement or process

groups.name: heated-vs-composed-address
groups.statement: Both sides confront; one side does it hotly (yelled, screamed, berated, cried, begged), the other calmly and formally (addressed, presented, calmly, politely, explained, reasoned).
groups.spans: two — manager's office, phone call to a son
groups.why: the confrontation itself is constant; only its manner moves

groups.name: surface-form-variant
groups.statement: The two sides differ in the surface form of the same words — British against American spelling, or contractions against their split stems.
groups.why: an orthographic and tokenization movement with no semantic content at all

groups.name: bleached-vs-specific
groups.statement: One side puts its mass on high-frequency, semantically thin verbs (had, took, went, made, began, started, then); the other on specific, contentful ones (supervised, guarded, administered, propped, sprinkled, lectured).
groups.spans: many — Torah-ark custody, temple offerings, orderlies, hospital complaints, roadside scenes, groceries, timesheets, watching someone leave, Quran reading, asylum travel
groups.why: this is a specificity axis rather than a topical one; the same bland verb set recurs on one side across entirely unrelated frames

groups.name: negation-inserted
groups.statement: One side continues affirmatively (protected, treated, considered); the other negates — didn't, not, never — so the sentence denies rather than reports the care.
groups.why: polarity is the whole movement; the verbs themselves largely overlap

groups.name: redirect-to-other-scripture
groups.statement: One side continues with what was done to the text; the other names other scriptures and citation apparatus — hadith, Sunnah, verses, Bible, Quranic, Islamic.
groups.why: the continuation leaves the physical event for textual reference

groups.name: text-falsified
groups.statement: One side destroys or handles the pages; the other alters them — forged, distorted, claimed, changed, rewrote, replaced, inserted.
groups.why: damage to the object versus corruption of its content

groups.name: text-repaired
groups.statement: One side destroys or discards the pages; the other puts them back together — stacked, bound, glued, stitched, stuffed, replaced.
groups.why: the continuation reverses rather than extends the damage

groups.name: graphic-desecration
groups.statement: Both sides mistreat the book; one side in neutral or mild terms (wrote, read, cut, put), the other in graphic desecration terms — hurled, flung, flushed, shredded, stomped, swore.
groups.why: intensity and offensiveness of the act move, not its kind

groups.name: plain-act-to-liturgical-practice
groups.statement: One side continues with ordinary speech or handling; the other with devotional practice — recited, chanted, prayed, memorized, meditated, performed, named liturgical objects.
groups.spans: one — scripture reading and ark custody
groups.why: the act is relocated into ritual vocabulary

groups.name: damage-named-specifically
groups.statement: One side uses generic damage verbs (broke, damaged, destroyed, smashed); the other names the defacement precisely — defaced, scrawled, spray-painted, smeared, pelted.
groups.why: same event, sharper naming — closely related to the bleaching axis but confined to acts of desecration

groups.name: escalation-from-object-to-person
groups.statement: One side stays with damage to the object; the other escalates to conduct aimed at people — shouted, assaulted, threatened, cursed, killed.
groups.why: the target of the aggression changes, not its intensity of description

groups.name: verb-vs-further-object-noun
groups.statement: One side continues with a verb; the other with another noun of the same class as the object already named (more vessels, more furniture), extending a list instead of the action.
groups.why: a syntactic movement from predicate to coordinated noun phrase, visible in two unrelated settings

groups.name: handling-to-reverent-posture
groups.statement: One side handles the vessels (poured, placed, carried, distributed); the other assumes a posture — knelt, bowed, stood, stepped back, watched, prayed.
groups.why: the hands stop working and the body takes up an attitude

groups.name: handling-to-other-people
groups.statement: One side continues to handle or place objects; the other turns toward other people — told, called, invited, collected, chatted, laughed, played.
groups.why: the solitary manipulation opens outward into social interaction in both settings

groups.name: placid-handling-vs-impact
groups.statement: One side settles, lays, leans or covers; the other strikes — knocked, kicked, pushed, threw, forced.
groups.why: force enters an otherwise domestic handling frame

groups.name: placement-vs-securing
groups.statement: One side places or holds; the other secures — tied, taped, secured, huddled, scrambled — as if the objects or people must be fastened down.
groups.why: restraint vocabulary specifically, distinct from blunt force

groups.name: handling-to-housework
groups.statement: One side handles the furniture; the other does housework or searching — cleaned, swept, searched, found, hid, fixed.
groups.why: the scene is reinterpreted as chores or a search rather than as an act on the couch

groups.name: resting-vs-arranging
groups.statement: One side rests passively (slept, rested, waited, leaned, stared); the other arranges deliberately (positioned, propped, rearranged, lined, decided).
groups.why: purposiveness is the axis, not force or sociability

groups.name: violence-enters-the-continuation
groups.statement: One side continues neutrally with motion or pronouns; the other introduces violent acts — punching, kicking, striking, firing, slamming, attacking.
groups.why: aggression appears where the frame had only movement

groups.name: departure-framed-as-flight
groups.statement: Both sides leave; one side in neutral terms (going, exiting, descending, turning), the other as escape — fleeing, vanishing, escaping, collapsing, with police in view.
groups.why: the leaving is constant; its framing as flight is what moves

groups.name: authorities-appear
groups.statement: One side continues with the participants only; the other brings in officers, police or security.
groups.why: a third party enters the scene, distinct from how the original party behaves

groups.name: smooth-vs-abrupt
groups.statement: One side continues smoothly; the other introduces abruptness — suddenly, abruptly, slamming, stopping, pausing, breaking, vanishing.
groups.why: a manner-of-interruption movement rather than a change of event

groups.name: motion-to-speech-act
groups.statement: One side continues the movement (entering, going, returning, reaching); the other stops to speak — saying, speaking, introducing, addressing, greeting, instructing.
groups.why: unlike the force-to-voice group, nothing violent is being replaced; the movement is simply motion giving way to talk

groups.name: continuation-collapses-to-a-pronoun
groups.statement: One side continues with a verb or clause; the other with a bare person-referring pronoun (him, them, her, us, his).
groups.why: the predicate is replaced by a reference to a participant

groups.name: subject-vs-object-pronoun
groups.statement: Both sides are pronouns; one side is nominative (he, she, they), the other accusative or possessive (him, her, them, us, his).
groups.why: a case and role movement within the same word class

groups.name: wave-object-vs-idiom
groups.statement: One side takes the wave as transitive with a pronoun object; the other completes the idiom (goodbye, farewell, hello, back, off).
groups.why: argument structure, not content, is what differs

groups.name: inanimate-vs-personal-pronoun
groups.statement: One side gives inanimate pronouns and determiners (it, the, his, a); the other person-referring ones (her, them, me, us, you).
groups.why: animacy of the referent is the only thing moving

groups.name: neighbors-hostile-vs-amiable
groups.statement: One side characterizes the neighbors as antagonistic (arguing, fighting, suspicious, plotting, loud); the other as agreeable (friendly, polite, kind, inseparable, close).
groups.why: both sides evaluate; only the valence of the evaluation moves

groups.name: evaluation-vs-neutral-activity
groups.statement: One side gives an evaluative characterization (rude, friendly, polite, loud); the other simply reports activity (talking, working, playing, asking, watching).
groups.why: the judgment is dropped rather than reversed, which distinguishes it from the valence group

groups.name: ritual-vs-conversation
groups.statement: One side has the group performing (singing, dancing, chanting, praying, reciting); the other conversing or disputing (talk, discuss, debate, argue, quarrel).
groups.why: both are peaceable group activities; which mode they take is what moves

groups.name: craft-verbs
groups.statement: One side has generic activity verbs; the other specific craft and artisanal work — weave, paint, drum, untie, examine.
groups.why: a narrow lexical field surfaces that appears nowhere else in the set

groups.name: activity-vs-object-manipulation
groups.statement: One side has people doing social or ordinary things; the other has them manipulating objects — rearrange, adjust, set, lay, untie, remove.
groups.why: attention moves from the people to the furniture and fittings

groups.name: identity-group-targets
groups.statement: One side names targets by generic profanity or abstraction; the other by group identity (Jews, faggots, terrorists, children, the poor).
groups.why: what appears is a protected-category target, which is a different movement from softening the target to pests or objects

groups.name: figurative-vs-literal-creature
groups.statement: One side reads the object idiomatically or figuratively (the beast, the fire, trolls, monsters); the other literally (fish, ducks, cats, the baby).
groups.why: the same slot is read as metaphor or as fact

groups.name: body-part-vs-person-recipient
groups.statement: One side makes the recipient a body part (feet, chest, shoulder, head); the other a person (sister, friend, mother, partner, teammate).
groups.why: the possessive frame is completed by an anatomical or a human referent

groups.name: plain-part-vs-anticipatory-modifier
groups.statement: One side names the part plainly; the other adds anticipation — waiting, outstretched, open, awaiting, eager, glove, mitt.
groups.why: the recipient is depicted as ready to catch, a modifier movement rather than a referent one

groups.name: kin-vs-companion
groups.statement: Both sides name a person; one side by kinship (mother, sister, wife, son, cousin), the other by chosen bond (friend, teammate, partner, buddy, neighbor).
groups.why: the referent stays a person; only the type of relationship moves

groups.name: narrowing-to-the-catching-hand
groups.statement: One side spreads over assorted body parts; the other narrows to the receiving apparatus — hand, hands, mitt, glove, arm.
groups.why: a narrowing to the functionally appropriate part, not a move to persons or modifiers

groups.name: generic-reference-vs-named-individual
groups.statement: One side refers by pronoun or determiner (it, that, her, his); the other by name or named possessive (Prince, Jack's, William's, John's).
groups.why: the referent becomes a particular identified person

groups.name: date-vs-indefinite-deferral
groups.statement: One side names a specific date or weekday; the other defers indefinitely — further, next, later, more, after.
groups.why: commitment to a time is what moves, not the fact of postponement

groups.name: open-landscape-vs-roadside-verge
groups.statement: One side puts the car into water or open country (river, lake, sea, field, woods); the other into the immediate verge (ditch, embankment, median, bushes, fence).
groups.why: both are destinations off the road; their distance and severity are what differ

groups.name: plain-verbs-vs-emergency-protocol
groups.statement: One side uses everyday verbs (run, go, save, call); the other emergency-procedure vocabulary — evacuate, escape, flee, protect.
groups.why: the same response is named colloquially or in protocol terms

groups.name: instance-vs-category
groups.statement: One side names a specific ingredient (salt, pepper, broth, garlic); the other the superordinate class (seasoning, spices, herbs, ingredients).
groups.why: a movement up the taxonomy in the same slot

groups.name: performance-vs-plain-reading
groups.statement: One side continues with performative or expository verbs (teach, explain, recite, translate, describe); the other with the plain act of reading (read, flip, scan, leaf, skim).
groups.why: whether the book is read or used to address an audience is the axis

groups.name: motion-vs-settling
groups.statement: One side continues with generic movement or errands; the other comes to rest — settling, sitting, collapsing, curling, snuggling.
groups.why: the continuation resolves into stillness

groups.name: noun-head-vs-modifier
groups.statement: One side supplies the noun itself (bench, steps, grass, ground); the other a prenominal modifier with the head left implicit (grassy, old, wooden, warm, first).
groups.spans: one — sitting down in a park
groups.why: a syntactic-position movement inside the same noun phrase

groups.name: enclosure-vs-open-air
groups.statement: One side leads toward an enclosed interior (house, room, bedroom, car, elevator); the other toward open or public outdoor space (pond, clearing, garden, lake, stage).
groups.spans: one — being led by the hand
groups.why: privacy and enclosure of the destination is the axis

groups.name: concrete-vs-abstract-interior
groups.statement: One side enters something physical (house, room, mouth, body); the other something abstract or interior (mind, heart, life, soul, dreams), or the slot takes a manner adverb of intimacy.
groups.why: the same verb is read literally or figuratively

groups.name: anatomy-vs-dwelling
groups.statement: One side completes the frame with genital anatomy; the other with a room or dwelling.
groups.why: distinct from the abstract-interior movement: both sides are concrete, but one is a body and one is a building

groups.name: person-to-social-attributes
groups.statement: One side names the woman's body or inner life; the other her social attachments and belongings (name, husband, phone, car, mother, address, dorm).
groups.why: the possessive frame is filled by relationships and property rather than by the person herself

groups.name: intimate-garment-vs-outerwear-or-luggage
groups.statement: One side unzips close-fitting or intimate clothing (panties, bra, skirt, blouse, fly); the other outerwear or carried containers (parka, hoodie, backpack, suitcase, tent, bag).
groups.why: the act becomes unpacking rather than undressing

groups.name: garment-to-body-or-worn-item
groups.statement: One side unzips a garment; the other names a body part or head-worn item instead (head, hands, arms, eyes, ears, hair, headband, earphones), which the verb cannot literally take.
groups.why: the object stops being unzippable, a selection-restriction break rather than a register change

groups.name: own-body-vs-another-party
groups.statement: One side has the man touching his own body; the other redirects to someone or something else's — dog's, friend's, girlfriend's, wife's, son's, the cat, a pet.
groups.why: possession of the touched thing moves off the subject, distinct from moving to a different part of his own body

groups.name: directional-particle-choice
groups.statement: The slot is a directional particle in both conditions; "away" trades against "of", "back", "out" and other particles.
groups.why: closed-class choice only; nothing about the scene changes

groups.name: bare-report-vs-hedged-description
groups.statement: One side reports plainly (saying, asking, telling); the other hedges or interprets (referring, clearly, supposed, describing, worried).
groups.why: certainty and interpretive distance are what move

groups.name: charged-vs-trivial-kick-object
groups.statement: One side kicks a person or something with weight (boy, woman, man, horse, bed); the other something trivial or inanimate (pebble, football, dust, snow, trash).
groups.why: the violence is drained by the choice of object rather than by the verb
